At the Goleta Point site, the gooseneck barnacle Pollicipes polymerus attains a maximum capitulum height of 1.75 centimeters [Li = 1.75 centimeters], a size that reflects the local environmental conditions of this coastal exposure. Field surveys indicate that individuals there reach the onset of gonadal activity, characterized by the first development of viable gametes, at a capitulum height of 1.2 centimeters [Lp = 1.2 centimeters]. These measurements contrast with observations from a more northern locality, Holy, where the species achieves a substantially larger ultimate capitulum height of 3.25 centimeters [Li = 3.25 centimeters]. The larger body size at Holy is likely a consequence of cooler, more productive waters that support extended somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive effort. Puberty at this location corresponds to a capitulum height of 1.6 centimeters [Lp = 1.6 centimeters], indicating a later onset of sexual maturation relative to the Goleta Pt. population. Such intraspecific variation in size at maturity aligns with latitudinal clines documented in other sessile marine invertebrates, where slower growth rates at higher latitudes often delay reproductive maturation until a larger body size is achieved.

The reproductive potential of a gravid individual under optimal thermal conditions is considerable. At a stable water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a single berried female produces roughly 240,000 fertilized ova per brood event [N_R_i = roughly 240,000 fertilized ova per brood event], a fecundity that, combined with an average of seven broods annually [F_R_i = seven broods annually], translates into an estimated 1.68 million offspring per year — a strategy designed to offset the extremely high mortality rates experienced during the planktonic larval phase. The energetic cost of producing such a vast number of subitaneous eggs is substantial, and the sustained investment across multiple consecutive broods likely imposes a physiological ceiling on both somatic growth and overall female longevity in this species.

The earliest life stages are particularly vulnerable and small in size. Newly hatched nauplius larvae emerge weighing just 0.000000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000000524 grams] wet mass, a value derived from an average egg diameter of approximately 100 micrometers. This minuscule birth mass necessitates a prolonged period of planktonic development before the larva reaches the competency stage required for benthic settlement. The age at which the nauplius hatches from the brood egg, measured as the time since gamete fusion, is approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days] when incubation proceeds at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This length of embryonic development is consistent with the relatively low metabolic rates typical of cold-water crustacean eggs, where yolk-dependent growth proceeds slowly but steadily. Once hatched, the early nauplius must immediately commence exogenous feeding on phytoplankton, initiating a trophic switch from endogenous to external nutrient sources that sustains the rapid growth of the accelerating larva.

Larval development culminates in the critical process of benthic settlement, during which the planktonic nauplius undergoes a profound metamorphosis to adopt a sessile, filter-feeding juvenile morphology. The time since birth that elapses before the larva settles onto a hard substrate is 42 days  at a rearing temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This relatively protracted settlement delay reflects the need for the pre-metamorphic larva to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves and undergo the necessary body plan reorganisation to survive the transition from pelagic to benthic life. Following metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic juvenile faces a period of intense growth and competitive pressure for space in the intertidal zone. Survivorship during this early benthic phase is notoriously low, though those recruits that successfully secure a favorable microhabitat can eventually reach reproductive maturity and contribute to the next generation.

The overall pace of the gooseneck barnacle life cycle is remarkably slow, with individuals exhibiting an extreme maximum lifespan that places Pollicipes polymerus among the longest-lived cirripedes known. The oldest documented specimens reach an age of 20 years [am = 20 years] when residing at a constant water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], far exceeding the typical 2–5 year lifespan of most intertidal barnacles. Such longevity indicates that individuals continue to grow and add capitulum height incrementally throughout their lives, only achieving full asymptotic size after roughly two decades. The species thus invests heavily in somatic durability and iterative reproductive output over an extended period rather than maturing rapidly and reproducing in a single, intense burst. This life-history strategy, built around high annual fecundity, a protracted larval phase, and extreme adult longevity, is well suited to the unpredictable but consistently productive intertidal environment, where space and food availability can fluctuate considerably across seasons and years.
